common_name: Emily McKenzie Crocosmia (Orange-Red Bicolor with Dark Throat)

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Emily McKenzie is a classic older crocosmia cultivar producing burnt-orange flowers each marked with a bold, dark mahogany-red blotch at the base of each petal, a distinctive bicolor eye pattern unlike the solid-color flowers of many other crocosmia cultivars, held on arching sprays above bold, sword-like foliage in mid to late summer. The tubular flowers are a strong draw for hummingbirds and also make good, long-lasting cut flowers. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time; mulch over the corms for winter protection in the colder part of its range.

George Davison is an old, long-cultivated crocosmia selection bearing clear golden-yellow flowers on arching sprays above bold, sword-like foliage in mid to late summer, a cheerful, sunny color that stands apart from the more common orange and red crocosmia cultivars. Its more compact stature than taller crocosmia cultivars suits it to the front or middle of a mixed border, and the tubular flowers draw hummingbirds and make good cut flowers. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time.

Solfatare is one of the oldest named crocosmia cultivars still in commerce, dating to the 1880s, valued as much for its bronze-tinted foliage as for its soft apricot-yellow flowers, which are held on gracefully arching sprays in mid to late summer above the smoky-bronze, sword-like leaves. The combination of warm foliage color and soft flower tone gives it a more subdued, sophisticated look than the vivid reds and oranges of most crocosmia cultivars, pairing well with other bronze- or burgundy-foliaged perennials. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time.

common_name: Night Embers Daylily (Dark Red Velvet Daylily)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in spring or fall; set crowns just 1 in below soil level in full sun to light afternoon shade.

directions: Plant fans with the crown about 1 in deep, spreading roots outward over a small mound of soil in the hole, and water thoroughly after planting. Night Embers bears deep, velvety wine-red flowers with a darker red eye zone and a faint gold edge picking up the light, a rich, smoldering color that gives the cultivar its name, blooming heavily over a long midseason display. Its dark, saturated color reads best against a lighter background — pale gravel, light-colored mulch, or silver-foliaged companions — where the depth of the red is not lost in shadow. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines, and remove spent scapes after all buds open to keep the planting tidy.

common_name: Siloam June Bug Daylily (Chartreuse-Green Siloam Series Daylily)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in spring or fall; set crowns just 1 in below soil level in full sun to light afternoon shade.

directions: Plant fans with the crown about 1 in deep, spreading roots outward over a small mound of soil in the hole, and water thoroughly to settle the soil. Part of the celebrated Siloam breeding line developed by Pauline Henry, Siloam June Bug bears unusual chartreuse-green flowers with a deeper green throat, a color rarely seen in daylilies and one that reads almost lime-yellow in bright light, on a compact, dwarf-scale plant. Its small stature and unusual color make it a distinctive accent in a mixed border or collector's daylily bed, standing apart from the more common pink, red, and gold Siloam introductions. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines.

Designer Gown bears large, heavily ruffled, cream-to-pale-pink flowers with a delicate, almost fabric-like texture to the ruffled petal edges, giving each bloom an elegant, dressy appearance that inspired its name. Its soft, romantic coloring and ruffled form make it a strong choice for cottage-garden and cutting-garden plantings alongside other pastel-toned perennials. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines, and remove spent scapes after all buds open to keep the planting tidy.

common_name: White Queen Crinum (Large Pure White Crinum Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the plant room to form a substantial clump over time. White Queen bears large, pure white, fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers held in dramatic clusters atop tall stalks above broad, strap-like foliage, one of the showiest white-flowered crinum lilies grown in Southern gardens. Established clumps are extremely tough and long-lived, tolerating heat, humidity, and drought once settled in, though regular moisture and feeding during the growing season improve bloom. Crinums resent disturbance, so once planted, leave the clump undisturbed for years to reach full size and flowering potential, dividing only when significantly overcrowded.

common_name: Music Box Sunflower (Compact Multicolor Branching Dwarf Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; for succession harvests, sow every 1–2 weeks through summer.

directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in full sun after last frost, spacing plants 10–14 inches apart. Music Box is a dwarf, heavily branching sunflower producing an abundance of smaller, 4–6 inch flowers in a full mix of colors — gold, yellow, mahogany, and bicolor combinations — on compact plants that stay under 3 feet, making it well suited to containers, border edges, and small gardens where full-size single-stem sunflowers would be too large. Unlike single-stem cut-flower types, its branching habit means one plant produces many flowers over an extended period rather than a single bloom all at once, giving a longer season of color in the garden. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continued branching and bloom through summer into fall.
